newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba official says EMU needs small start group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba official says EMU needs small start group.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen took the hardline on Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) on Friday, saying the euro could only be launched on time if limited to a small group of countries.

Jochimsen also said it made no sense to categorically rule out delaying EMU beyond the politically-cherished January 1 1999 deadline, echoing the ambiguous line on the timetable taken by Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer this week.

A lot of work remained to be done before countries got their finances in order for Maastricht, but at the same time softening the qualification criteria or choosing participants on the basis of a "gentlemen's agreement" was unthinkable.

"If the deadline set out in the treaty is to be kept, but if on the other hand there is to be no decision at the euro's expense, it follows that only a start with a small circle of really qualified countries can be considered," Jochimsen said in a speech delivered in Luxembourg but made available here.
A broader EMU start would of necessity require a softening of the tough but essential criteria countries must meet to take part, he warned.

The toughest of the Maastricht criteria, and so far the Achilles heel for many countries including Germany, concern budgets. The treaty calls on states to keep budget deficits at no more than three percent of gross domestic product and debt levels at no more than 60 percent of GDP.
Jochimsen said Germany, one of the linchpins of EMU, would have an extremely tough job to meet these demands.

Even if this week's forecast by the top six economic institutes that Germany's 1997 budget deficit would be three to 3.2 percent of GDP proves accurate, "that would just be an on the spot fulfilment, and thus in no way the lasting, sustainable budgetary discipline the contract demands."
Jochimsen said political considerations should play no part in deciding who takes part in monetary union and said such a ploy "will not and cannot work."
"Anyone can bring up some kind of excuses and explanations. Therefore I say very clearly: All candidates must be judged by the same measure," he said.

Bundesbank officials have been very vocal on the subject of monetary union this week and Tietmeyer in particular attracted interest when he said on Monday that a delay to the project could be considered if large countries failed to qualify.
The Bundesbank president on Thursday watered down that position, saying he had only meant it would not be a catastrophe from a technical perspective if the euro launch were delayed.

Jochimsen said calls for immediate negotiations on a delayed start for the euro were "wrong" and risked disrupting the pressure on countries to pursue budgetary consolidation measures which were necessary whatever happened.

Moreover, he said it was impossible to say with certainty what could develop on budgetary positions between now and Spring 1998 when the decision on which countries are qualified to launch the euro is scheduled to be taken.
"On the other hand a delayed start should not be ruled out categorically in advance or even demonised as a 'question of war and peace'," Jochimsen said.
"It would be totally absurd to place a general ban on thinking and discussion as a form of political correctness."
Jochimsen said the choice of EMU starters would become an increasingly hot issue, particularly as "supposed favourites" looked like failing to make the Maastricht grade.

But he said that talk of "dying for Maastricht", a phrase referring to the hardships provoked by spending cuts in preparation for the project and which he said was as current in Germany as in the "Club Med" countries, was nonsensical.
"Make no mistake, consolidating household positions, cutting borrowing and interest payments are the needs of the moment, totally independently of Maastricht."
